spec.credit: UPSC CSE (Main) 2025 · Economics optional Paper I · Q4(c)
spec.text: Define money multiplier and discuss its determinants. Explain in terms of money multiplier, how the banking system of an economy can control money supply.

scenes.vo: UPSC, twenty twenty-five. Economics optional, Paper One, fifteen marks. Define money multiplier and discuss its determinants. Then explain how the banking system can control money supply. Here's the trap. The formula most people write first is only true in a world with no cash.
scenes.visual: The printed question on a paper card, credit line 'UPSC CSE (Main) 2025, Economics Paper I, Q4(c)'. The words 'define', 'determinants' and 'control money supply' glow faintly (plant).

spec.text: Define money multiplier and discuss its determinants. Explain in terms of money multiplier, how the banking system of an economy can control money supply.

directives.meaning: a precise meaning, with the formula

scenes.vo: Read what it asks. Define means a precise meaning, with the formula. Discuss means more than one side. So there are three jobs: the definition, the determinants, and how the system controls money.
scenes.visual: Question X-ray: 'Define', 'discuss' and 'Explain' underlined; three empty boxes D1 to D3 (plant: they tick at the end).

scenes.vo: Start with what NCERT shows. A bank must keep part of each deposit as reserves. Say twenty percent. A hundred rupees comes in. Eighty is lent, and comes back as a deposit somewhere else. Then sixty-four is lent, and so on.
scenes.visual: The lending rounds as stacked coins: 100, 80, 64, each smaller; a reserve jar fills.

scenes.vo: Add up the rounds, and a hundred rupees of reserves supports five hundred rupees of deposits. That five is the money multiplier. Here it is one over the reserve ratio.
scenes.visual: The rounds sum to 500; the label m = 5 = 1/0.2 appears.

scenes.vo: But people also keep cash. Every rupee held as cash stops a round. So the full formula has two ratios: cash to deposits, and reserves to deposits. In India, cash is about fifteen percent of deposits.
scenes.visual: A rupee leaks out of the chain into a wallet; the formula m = (cdr + 1)/(cdr + rr) writes itself.

blocks.text: The money multiplier (m) links the money supply (M) to high-powered money (H): M = m × H. H, also called reserve money, is the currency issued by the central bank, held by the public or by banks.
1. Definition and formula

With currency C, deposits D and bank reserves R: M = C + D and H = C + R, so m = (cdr + 1)/(cdr + rr), where cdr = C/D and rr = R/D. If no cash is held, m = 1/rr: at rr = 20%, ₹100 of reserves supports ₹500 of deposits (m = 5).
Lending rounds at a 20% reserve ratio: ₹100, ₹80, ₹64 … adding up to ₹500 of deposits.
blocks.label: Fig. 1: How ₹100 of reserves becomes ₹500 of deposits

blocks.text: 2. Determinants

• Reserve ratio (rr): set partly by RBI's CRR (3.00% of NDTL since November 2025) and SLR (18.00%); a higher rr lowers m. • Currency-deposit ratio (cdr): the public's taste for cash, about 15% in July 2026; a higher cdr lowers m. • Banks' willingness to lend and the demand for loans: profit, regulation and borrowers limit lending (Bundesbank, 2017). • Shocks: in 1930-1933 US money fell about 35% while the base rose about 20%, as people pulled cash from banks.
3. How the banking system controls money supply

• RBI changes H: buying bonds in the open market adds reserves; selling them drains reserves. • RBI changes rr: a higher CRR makes banks cut lending, so m and M fall. • The policy rate (repo 5.50%) is today's main lever, working through banks' lending decisions. • Banks create deposits when they lend; the multiplier is the outer limit, not a constant.
So M = m × H: RBI steers H, the reserve ratio and the policy rate, while people's cash habits and banks' lending decide how far the multiplier really works.

scenes.vo: Now we write. No word limit is printed, so we set our own: about two hundred and fifty words in eleven minutes. Open with the definition in one line: the money supply is the multiplier times high-powered money.
scenes.visual: The answer sheet; clock 11:00 and word counter 0. The introduction writes in.

scenes.vo: Section two is the determinants. The reserve ratio, which RBI sets partly through the CRR, now three percent. The public's taste for cash. Banks' willingness to lend. And shocks: in the Great Depression, people pulled cash from banks, and America's money shrank.

weak.miss: only true with no cash held; the full formula has the currency-deposit ratio

weak.text: With today's CRR the multiplier is about 33.3.
weak.miss: a toy ceiling; real lending is capped by more than the CRR
leaves out the public's cash habits and banks' wish to lend

weak.text: RBI controls money supply through the multiplier.
weak.miss: no mechanism: H, rr and the policy rate are never named
a definition question that never shows the ₹100 → ₹500 rounds

scenes.vo: Now the easy answer beside it. It writes one over CRR, and stops. It says today's multiplier is about thirty-three. It lists only CRR and SLR. It never says how control works. And there is no worked example.
